title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: When he got home, Vronsky found a note from Anna waiting. She wrote: "I am ill and unhappy. I can't come out, but I can't go any longer without seeing you. Come this evening. Alexey Alexandrovitch goes to the council at seven and will be there till ten." He paused for a moment over the strangeness of her telling him to come straight to her, in spite of her husband's insistence that she not receive him, then decided to go.

Vronsky had gotten his promotion that winter; he was now a colonel, had left the regimental quarters, and was living on his own. After a quick lunch he lay down on the sofa, and within five minutes memories of the hideous scenes he had witnessed over the past few days blurred together with a mental image of Anna and of the peasant who had played such a part in the bear hunt, and Vronsky fell asleep. He woke in the dark, trembling with horror, and hurriedly lit a candle. "What was that? What? What was the terrible thing I dreamed? Yes, yes — I think a little dirty man with a disheveled beard was stooping over, doing something, and all at once he began saying some strange words in French. Yes — there was nothing else in the dream," he said to himself. "But why was it so awful?" He saw the peasant again, vividly, and the incomprehensible French words the peasant had spoken, and a chill of horror ran down his back.
"What nonsense!" Vronsky thought, and looked at his watch.

It was already half past eight. He rang for his servant, dressed in a hurry, and went out onto the steps, forgetting the dream entirely and worried only about being late. As he drove up to the Karenins' entrance he looked at his watch and saw it was ten minutes to nine. A high, narrow carriage with a pair of grays stood at the door. He recognized Anna's carriage. "She's coming to me," Vronsky thought, "and better that she should. I don't like going into that house. But no matter; I can't hide." And with that manner he had had since boyhood, of a man who has nothing to be ashamed of, Vronsky stepped out of his sledge and went to the door. The door opened, and the hall-porter with a rug on his arm called the carriage forward. Vronsky, though he didn't usually notice small things, noticed at that moment the amazed look the porter shot at him. In the doorway itself Vronsky nearly collided with Alexey Alexandrovitch. The gas jet threw its full light on the bloodless, sunken face under the black hat and on the white cravat shining against the beaver of the coat. Karenin's fixed, dull eyes were fastened on Vronsky's face. Vronsky bowed, and Alexey Alexandrovitch, chewing his lips, lifted his hand to his hat and walked on. Vronsky watched, without turning his head, as he got into the carriage, picked up the rug and the opera-glass from the window, and disappeared. Vronsky went into the hall. His brows were knotted, and his eyes glittered with a proud, angry light.

"What a position!" he thought. "If he would fight, if he would stand up for his honor, I could act, I could express what I feel; but this weakness or baseness.... He puts me in the position of playing false, which I never meant and never mean to do."

Vronsky's thinking had changed since the day of his conversation with Anna in the Vrede garden. Unconsciously yielding to Anna's weakness — she had surrendered herself completely to him and simply looked to him to decide her fate, ready to submit to anything — he had long since stopped thinking their tie might end as he had thought back then. His ambitious plans had retreated into the background again, and feeling that he had stepped outside the circle of activity in which everything was definite, he had given himself entirely to his passion, and that passion was binding him more and more closely to her.
He was still in the hall when he caught the sound of her retreating footsteps. He knew she had been waiting for him, listening for him, and was now going back to the drawing-room.
"No," she cried when she saw him, and at the first sound of her voice the tears came into her eyes. "No; if it's going to go on like this, the end will come much, much too soon."

"What? I've been waiting in agony for an hour, two hours.... No, I won't.... I can't quarrel with you. Of course you couldn't come. No, I won't." She laid her two hands on his shoulders and looked at him for a long time with a deep, passionate, searching look. She was studying his face to make up for the time she had not seen him. Every time she saw him, she was bringing the picture of him she carried in her imagination (incomparably better, impossible in reality) into line with him as he really was.
